items.content:
Just wrapped up a fantastic week in Montreal speaking at the International Institute of Forecasters (ISF 2026).

I had the privilege of presenting on a topic: why technically correct forecasts still fail. And weaved in a little bit about culture and sold out of my books. Was shocked and very very humbling to even hear a premiere professor from Hong Kong Polytechnic quoting me from the stage 

One thing the week reinforced for me is a gap our profession still has the opportunity to close. I didnt understand half of what i heard but flip side many of them didnt hear or truly understand the message I was saying either. 

On one side, there is some incredible academic research pushing forecasting science forward. And then there was some totally disconnected from reality or papers for thr sake of a paper. 

On the other side, working with companies around the world, they have their own issues of being disconnected. I see them default to "the way we've always done it" instead of giving new ideas the opportunity to prove themselves in the real world. 

In this AI expectations bubble we may be living this gap between academic and practitioner is growing wider. 

Researchers need practitioners to validate, challenge, and refine new ideas. Practitioners need researchers to keep pushing the boundaries of what's possible. Innovation happens when science and application meet.

Lets see where all of this goes and where all of us together in this field responsibly take it.

A sincere thank you to the organizers and Ying Fry Michael Gilliland and Dr. Sven F. Crone for inviting me to share with your community. I left with new perspectives, new friendships, and great conversations that will undoubtedly shape my own thinking.

items.content:
Your executive changes the forecast to the budget numbers. You know the number is wrong. What do you do?

Sales want a larger forecast to protect a customer relationship. Finance wants a lower number to protect cash. Operations want a stable or even lower number to avoid changing production and reduce inventory.

You are the demand planner. The evidence supports none of the three numbers completely, and the executive says to you “make the forecast work, just give me the right number”

Yes I train people around the world on best practices of unconstrained and unbiased forecasts, consensus processes, and one number attitude… but I also realize real world outside of textbooks and was practitioner for years and have scars to prove it.

The problem is best practice usually has nuance and there aren’t always clear answers. There are only assumptions, trade-offs, and risk.

This is why I've always believed the most valuable skill in planning isn't forecasting. It's facilitating better business decisions.

So here's my question..  What would you do? And not the textbook answer (I know those) no what do you do in the company with these pressures, with your fear of telling the boss they are wrong or upsetting sales or operations who don’t trust you anyway. 

You’re the forecaster: “make the forecast work, just give me the right number”

👇 I'd genuinely like to hear how your organization handles this.

items.content:
OpenAI's AI went rogue.  How is that for clickbait.

But I think many people are taking away the wrong lesson.

OpenAI wasn't asking the AI to be a helpful chatbot and make you happy. It was intentionally testing an AI agent designed to find vulnerabilities and achieve a cybersecurity objective while solving for a test. During that evaluation, the system aggressively pursued its assigned goal in ways the researchers did not anticipate.

The important question isn't... "Why did AI become evil?" It's... "Did we define the objective correctly?"

This is a lesson supply chain professionals, planners, and executives need to be careful of.

Goodhart's Law states: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

AI doesn't understand your business objective. It optimizes the reward function you give it. Reward functions are proxies, not perfect representations of success. AI eventually exploits the proxy rather than achieving the true objective

If your reward is "solve this problem," or “reduce forecast error” don't be surprised when it finds a shortcut you never intended that doesn’t solve the problem you actually intended.

That's not AI "going rogue." That's AI doing exactly what it was optimized to do.

Most AI today is highly specialized and capable within its objective. 

The lesson from this week's incident isn't that machines have become self-aware. It's that as AI becomes more capable, defining the right objective becomes just as important as building a better model. The biggest risk isn't AI thinking for itself. It's humans asking AI to optimize the wrong thing.

YES or NO???

One interesting cultural nuance:

In Italy, conversations are often highly interactive. It's common to end a statement with "no?" as a way of directly inviting confirmation or agreement.

In many Chinese business conversations, it's less interactive and silence is often comfortable and shows consideration and they need to be asked directly for confirmation. But many times, "yes" often means "I hear you" rather than "I agree with you." It's an acknowledgment before it's an agreement.

Now imagine these cultures and colleagues working together.

That could be the beginning of perfect communication... or one of the biggest misunderstandings in global business.

Culture is fascinating.

[Mini Interview] A Life Dedicated to S&OP — Becoming One of the Field’s Most Influential Voices
 
Meet Eric Wilson, Director of Thought Leadership at the Institute of Business Forecasting & Planning (IBF), author of Beyond Borders, speaker, and advisor to Fortune 500 companies. He helps organizations and individuals improve forecasting, planning, and Sales & Operations Planning (S&OP/IBP) performance and growth.
 
 
Tell us about yourself? 
 
I came to my current point in my professional journey after couple decades of practitioner experience working in various industries and companies in transformational roles.
 
My career has been dedicated to growing our field, sharing, and helping organizations make better business decisions through forecasting, planning, and S&OP/IBP.
 
Currently I am a thought leader at IBF and develop educational programs and host the IBF On Demand podcast. I have authored several books and regularly speak at conferences on topics ranging from forecasting and analytics AI to organizational alignment.
 
I spend most of my time now training individuals and teams and advising and helping organizations bridge the gap between strategy and execution. I remain passionate about the human side of planning and how people with technology collaborate to make better decisions.
 
 
What are the Pros/Cons of S&OP?
 
The biggest benefit of S&OP/IBP is alignment. When done well, it creates a common set of assumptions that allows sales, operations, finance, and leadership to make coordinated decisions.
 
The challenge is that many organizations focus too heavily on the process, technology, or forecast and not enough on people.
 
One of the biggest myths is that S&OP is a supply chain process. It is actually a business process.
 
Another myth is that better software automatically creates better outcomes. In my experience, S&OP is fundamentally a social process. Success depends on collaboration, trust, transparency, and decision-making.
 
This becomes even more important in global organizations where cultural differences influence how people communicate, build consensus, and approach conflict.
 
 
What are your learnings from being the Voice of S&OP?
 
One lesson stands above all others: the best planning organizations are not necessarily the most sophisticated, they are the most aligned. Through years of research, interviews, and global experience, I have learned culture matters far more than most organizations realize.
 
These observations ultimately inspired my newest book, Beyond Borders, which explores how cultural complexity shapes global business processes and S&OP.
 
If I could offer three additional key learnings, they would be: focus on decisions, not meetings; invest in relationships as much as data; and remember that planning is not about predicting the future but preparing your organization to respond to it.
 
The organizations that master these principles consistently outperform those that focus only on tools and process.

S&OP is not just a process, it is a leadership capability.

My biggest takeaway: S&OP is far more than a monthly process for balancing demand and supply.

At its best, it is a business management capability that connects strategy to execution, aligns commercial, operations, finance and supply chain teams around shared assumptions, and enables faster, better-informed decisions.

From a supply chain consulting perspective, four themes stood out for me:

Technology and AI improve visibility, scenario modelling and decision-making speed, but they cannot compensate for poor data quality, unclear governance or weak collaboration.
- Technology and AI improve visibility, scenario modelling and decision-making speed, but they cannot compensate for poor data quality, unclear governance or weak collaboration.
- Resilience is built before disruption occurs. It requires scenario thinking, clear decision rights and a planning cadence that turns insight into action.
- The "one-number" mindset is not about forcing consensus; it is about fostering transparency, constructive challenge and accountability.
- Executive ownership is the difference between S&OP being a reporting exercise and becoming a true value-creation engine.

Thank you to Institute of Business Forecasting & Planning, ASCM, Eric Wilson, Abe Eshkenazi and all the speakers for sharing valuable insights and practical experiences across industries and maturity levels.

The question is no longer whether organisations need S&OP/IBP. The real question is: Does your process help leaders make better decisions when uncertainty increases?

Where do you see the biggest barrier to S&OP maturity today: data, process, technology or leadership alignment?

You don't need Claude Fable 5 for 90% of your work.
Here's how to use it for the other 10% without running out of money:

Most people switched over to Fable 5 the week it launched and never switched back.

That was fine while Anthropic was giving it away…unfortunately, we all need to pay now.

Almost nothing you do in a day needs the power of Fable 6. Emails, quick questions, cleaning up a draft, Opus and Sonnet can all of it and you won't notice the difference.

The 10% that does need it - the deep reasoning, the complex analysis - is worth setting up properly:

1/ Select the model

Open a new chat and pick "Fable 5" from the dropdown. 

Check your plan first, because some have it built in and everyone else is spending credits from the moment they select it.

2/ Choose a problem worth the money

Save it for multi-step work that needs real reasoning. Reviewing a financial report, comparing a bunch of docs, reading charts, PDFs and spreadsheets together in one go.

3/ Tell Claude your goal

Most people describe the task and stop. Add one line before the prompt instead: "When this is done, I need..." Give it a finished deliverable to work backwards from.

4/ Give clear instructions

Every strong Fable 5 prompt has 5 parts. The task, the reason it matters, who it's for, the sources to use, and the rules to follow. 

Miss those and Claude fills the gaps with assumptions, which is the most expensive kind of rewrite.

5/ Add your files

Click the + button in the lower left and upload everything relevant. Then say what each file is for. 

"Use File A for the prices." "Use File B for the customer feedback." Pointed instructions beat a pile of attachments every time.

6/ Set the effort level

This is the dial that actually controls your spend. It sits behind the model name next to the send button and you can change it mid-conversation. 

Keep it low for work that doesn't need a long review, and move it higher when the task has many stages, difficult decisions, large amounts of source material, or numbers that have to be right.

7/ Review the plan

If you're running this in Claude Code, a panel shows exactly what it intends to do before it starts. Glance at it every time. 

Catching a mistake there costs you nothing, and catching it in the finished file costs you the whole run.

8/ Expect auto switching

The model will automatically move over if you're in a certain niche, but don't worry, this happens in ~5% of cases.

For your every day work, Opus and Sonnet are great. But if you are going to use Fable, taking a few minutes to set it up well could save you hundreds.

5 months ago, my wife quit her $250,000/year job to work with me.
Here are my biggest reflections:

The first few weeks had some bumps. We had to figure out who owned what, how to give each other feedback at work, and what our roles actually were. Since then it has been amazing. I couldn't wish for a better partner.

4 things we've learned in 5 months:

1/ You cannot leave things unsaid.

At a normal job, you can sit on a small frustration and let it fade. When your business partner is your wife, that frustration comes home with you. So whenever we have disagreements, nothing gets left unsaid.

2/ Set norms for how you behave in front of the team.

For us, that means being professional. Our team should see 2 colleagues, not a couple fighting over stupid sh*t.

3/ Lean into each other's strengths.

Our brains work completely differently. Her mind naturally runs across everything at once, so she keeps the whole operation moving. I go super deep on a few things at a time. If we were the same, one of us would be redundant.

4/ It adds a depth to your relationship that I didn't expect.

In business, there is always a new challenge to think through. It's like having a puzzle to work on together every single day. We have an endless list of things to talk about. And that makes it so incredibly fun!

What else do you want to know about working with your partner?

Claude launched a new model yesterday (Opus 5).
Now there are 4 to choose from. Here’s what to use when:

A quick email, a deep research project, and an end to end workflow shouldn't start with the same model.

Yet most people pick whichever one is on default and hope for the best.

Here's the simple guide I use instead:

1/ What They’e Built For

I think of them like four different hires. I wouldn't give the same task to a designer and a content strategist, so I don't send every task to the same model.

Haiku is built for fast, one-off tasks. Sonnet is the everyday model. Opus is made for complex enterprise work, and Fable is built for end to end workflows.

2/ Writing

Sonnet covers day to day emails and quick drafts. Fable is my pick when the draft has to follow my voice, specific instructions, and rules.

I use it for complex content where one missed detail makes the whole thing sound like generic AI copy.

3/ Research

Fable is what I reach for when I need deep research with sources, context, and different points of view.

Sonnet is faster when I have one clear question and need an answer I can use right away.

4/ Doc Analysis

Fable is best when the file is dense and every detail matters, like a contract or a filing.

For a normal spreadsheet or short document, Sonnet usually gives me what I need without making the task more complex.

5/ Skip It When

Every model has a wrong job too.

Skip Opus when the task is really simple. Skip Haiku when it's long and complex. Skip Sonnet when it's genuinely hard. And skip Fable when Sonnet can handle it.

6/ Brainstorming

I work with Sonnet to talk through an idea and push back and forth in real time. Haiku is enough for quick lists and captions.

Once the idea needs a proper strategy, more detail, or several angles, I move it into Fable.

7/ Context Window

Opus, Sonnet, and Fable can each hold 1M tokens of context. Haiku holds 200K.

That matters when I'm working with large docs, transcripts, examples, and feedback across a recurring project - the bigger the context window, the more the model can hold in its head at once.

The smartest model can be a waste on a simple job. And the fastest one can fall short on a hard one.

Spend five seconds choosing the right model before you spend twenty minutes fixing the answer - or get an invoice you regret later!

The biggest Claude mistake is sticking with a workflow that worked six months ago.
It slows you down and costs more tokens.

10 of them have simpler replacements now.

Here's where to start:

1/ Taking Claude's first draft as final

The first output is rarely the best one. Tell it exactly what's off, like "too formal" or "cut this by 30%". The next version gets much closer, and Claude gets smarter on what you want over time.

2/ Prompting without an audience in mind

Claude guesses when it doesn't know who will read the output. Spell out who it's for, what format it should be, and what it needs to achieve.

3/ Trusting every answer blindly

AI still gets things wrong with total confidence. Ask for sources or have it flag anything it's unsure about, then verify the claims that actually matter.

4/ Leaving Claude without a role

A generic assistant gives generic answers. Give it a persona to work from, like a sharp editor or a skeptical analyst, and the quality jumps immediately.

5/ Explaining your data in the prompt

Summarizing a spreadsheet by hand wastes time and loses detail. Drop the actual file in and let Claude run the numbers itself.

6/ Making charts and documents manually

Production work is exactly what Claude is good at. Describe what the finished piece should look like and it builds the file, chart, or doc for you.

7/ Treating one search as research

A single search answers small questions, and big ones need more. Research mode pulls from multiple sources and gives you a cited report.

8/ Ignoring Extended Thinking

The default setting is built for speed. Turn it on when a problem needs proper reasoning and you can see the logic behind every answer.

9/ Digging through old chats by hand

That conversation from three weeks ago is findable in seconds. Ask Claude to search your past chats and it pulls up the exact thread.

10/ Losing your best outputs in dead threads

Great work shouldn't vanish when the chat ends. Save the final version into the Project and Claude learns from it on the next run.

The habits that waste the most time often feel harmless.

But they take away hours every week by making tasks longer, heavier, and more complex.

items.content:
Most content is boring for 1 simple reason:


The writer takes too long to explain why anyone should care.

Most people write LinkedIn posts like they're telling a story at a dinner party.

But at a dinner party, people know who you are. They've agreed to spend the evening with you, and walking away halfway through a story would be a little rude. 

So you can take your time and give all the context you need.

On LinkedIn you get none of that. Strangers owe you nothing, and they can keep scrolling without giving you a second thought.

Your posts have to earn their attention.

Here's how anyone can do this:

1/ Open with proof

Start with a result, a number, or a real example. "I analyzed 200,000 posts" earns more attention than "Here are 5 LinkedIn tips" because the proof does the convincing before anyone even gets to the advice.

2/ Give people a reason to listen

Name the exact thing that earns the right to give this advice. I lean on my time at Goldman and my journey from 3,000 to 436K followers. That background is the one thing nobody can copy, even if they copy my content.

3/ Lead with the most surprising point

I write the full post before I write the hook. The strongest opening is usually buried halfway down the first draft, so I pull it to the top and build the rest of the post around it.

Most content is boring because it makes people wait to find out why it matters. 

Give them the reason first, and make it something they can check. A number, a result, a date, a name. Then they'll stay.

items.content:
You don’t NEED funding, a team, or an MBA.
Starting a business in 2026 can be simple as this:

There’s a misconception that you need to spend months on business plans, logos, and landing pages before ever talking to a customer.

It all feels like progress…but it’s not.

The only progress that counts is proof someone will pay. And then someone actually paying 🙂

This is the playbook to use to start your solo business today:

1/ Solve a pain you know firsthand

Pick a problem you've dealt with yourself and can explain in one sentence. If you can't, keep looking.

Saywhat started because I was spending too much time writing LinkedIn comments. I solved my own problem first.

2/ Match your skills to demand

Your niche sits at the overlap of what you're good at, what people already pay for, and where you have real experience.

Miss one of those three and you're chasing a trend you barely understand.

3/ Talk to real customers

Never ask "would you buy this?" People say yes to be polite - you won't get any substantive feedback here.

Ask how they solve it today, what it cost them last month, and what they've already tried that failed.

4/ Launch a waitlist

Post about the problem, not the product, and link to a signup page. The people replying in your DMs are your first customers.

200 signups means build it. Under 200 means rework the idea.

5/ Build your offer ladder

Start free with a lead magnet, then a low ticket course ($50 to $500), then cohorts at $1k to $5k, then done-for-you work at $5k+.

You only need the first rung someone will say yes to.

6/ Do outbound early

DM people who comment on your posts, view your profile, or past colleagues who fit your ICP.

Mention the problem you're working on and ask if they deal with it too.

7/ Use AI to protect your time

Don't let it build unsupervised or replace your customer conversations. Use it to stress-test ideas, train it on your voice, and keep the stack simple… Slack, Notion, Zapier, Claude.

That frees you up for the work only you can do.

8/ Build in public

Test one idea, share the process, listen to the feedback, improve. Run that loop enough times and your audience builds the business with you.

One painful problem + one honest customer...it's all you need to get started. I bet you can find both by next Saturday.

People say Gen Z are lazy.
I don't buy it.

My whole team at WM Media, apart from my wife Caroline, is Gen Z.
No one on my team is "lazy."

Like with anything, I think it's about setting the right expectations.

When I first started hiring, I was shy about our expectations. I'd soften the demanding parts of the job because I didn't want to scare good people away.

Now I do the opposite. Before anyone joins, I call them and tell them why they shouldn't work with me.

I tell them this is a job for someone who wants to be the best in the world at something. Like truly world class.

Our clients set that bar. We work with 2 public companies, several billion dollar companies, and some of the top VCs in the world.

On Friday, I was in a meeting with a client had to had to pop out for a sec because “that might be Sam Altman calling." 😅 These are people driving the future of technology forward. They don't clock out at 5pm. And when you're their trusted partner, you move, and learn, at their pace.

On top of that, everyone here is learning the dark arts of social media. That takes real work too.

So I'm upfront with everyone - this involves a lot of work and if you want a 9 to 5, you won't find it here.

The people who hear all of that and still want in know exactly what they're walking into.

Combine clear expectations with interesting work and good pay, and the result is a team that works hard and enjoys it.

Sugarcoat the interview and the mismatch doesn't go away. It just shows up a few months later, when it costs everyone more.
